Multi-omics has shifted from a methodological aspiration to a routine design choice in the life sciences. Simultaneous profiling of genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic and microbial layers captures interactions that no single assay can resolve, and the conceptual rationale for combining these layers is no longer in dispute [R54]. What has lagged behind this conceptual maturation, however, is the software infrastructure that researchers must actually use. In our assessment of the field, a typical multi-omics project now involves roughly five to seven data types and on the order of several thousand samples, with each analytical step admitting a dozen or more competing implementations; these figures are author estimates rather than findings cited from the literature. The tooling has accumulated faster than the standards that should govern it, and the result is an analytical gap that is no longer conceptual but infrastructural: researchers spend more time reconciling file formats, harmonizing object classes and reproducing someone else's R environment than they do interpreting biological signal.

The heterogeneity of the available tools is striking. On the R side, Bioconductor provides the foundational data structures, most notably MultiAssayExperiment, which offers coordinated representation, storage and operation on diverse genomics datasets and ships with ready-to-analyze TCGA objects [R28]; on top of this substrate the community has built package-specific integrators such as mixOmics with its DIABLO supervised framework [R27], the longitudinal timeOmics [R20] and netOmics packages [R21], the vertical and horizontal miodin workflow [R48], the MOFA-based transfer-learning extension MOTL [R32], the MuSA radiogenomic GUI built on the same MultiAssayExperiment class [R25], and reproducibility-oriented wrappers such as moiraine that preprocess data, run one or more integration methods and enable head-to-head comparison across integration tools [R3]. The Python ecosystem is no less crowded, ranging from graph-neural-network frameworks such as BioNeuralNet [R5] to specialised deep-learning integrators including MOADLN, which uses self-attention and a Multi-Omics Correlation Discovery Network to combine omics-specific encoders before classification [R17], MCluster-VAEs [R22], MO-GCAN [R29], DeepMoIC [R12] and MoAGL-SA [R39]. Parallel to these programmatic ecosystems, web-based point-and-click platforms have proliferated: the Analyst suite (ExpressAnalyst, MetaboAnalyst, OmicsNet, OmicsAnalyst) [R8], ExpOmics [R41], the single-cell analyst [R6], CFViSA, a free web platform integrating 79 tools with microbiome and transcriptome pipelines [R40], NOODAI [R33], PhenoMultiOmics [R14] and disease-specific portals such as CPMOAD [R7] and LOSTdb [R34] now offer GUI-driven alternatives that lower the barrier to entry but introduce their own concerns about transparency and reproducibility. Finally, containerised, workflow-management approaches — Nextflow, Snakemake and WorkflowHub-compatible Research Object Crates [R11, R18, R26, R35] — attempt to capture provenance at the level of the analysis environment itself.

Among these application domains, host–microbiome research exemplifies the infrastructural pressure particularly acutely. Microbial community samples bring together metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, metaproteomics and metabolomics, with sample coverage that is intrinsically inconsistent across layers because taxa differ in their genomic recoverability, expression detectability and chemical extractability [R1, R54]. As the microbial multi-omics perspective of Van Den Bossche and colleagues emphasises, the complexity of analysing a single isolate is multiplied further when samples comprise hundreds to thousands of individual species, yet standardised workflows and benchmarked datasets remain scarce [R54]. This combination — heterogeneous data formats, inconsistent sample coverage, complex analytical chains and weak reproducibility standards — illustrates the kind of field-level bottleneck that workflow-level solutions such as EasyMultiProfiler (EMP) attempt to address. EMP is an R workflow built on SummarizedExperiment and MultiAssayExperiment that organises extraction, preparation, support, analysis and visualisation into a single coherent pipeline [R1]. Microbiome multi-omics is therefore not just another application area; it is a particularly demanding setting in which any claim that multi-omics infrastructure has matured is put to the test.

A candid assessment must temper the cataloguing instinct. The sheer number of tools is often taken as evidence of progress, yet the evidence reviewed here describes a field in which each new publication tends to add another integration method rather than consolidate best practice. Benchmarking studies of cancer subtype clustering [R4], multi-omics biomarker discovery [R50] and single-cell integration [R10, R37] consistently find that no single method dominates across datasets, and that gains over simpler baselines are often modest. The persistence of batch effects, platform-specific artefacts and the absence of agreed-upon reference datasets mean that methodological choice — not biological signal — frequently determines the headline result. Tool catalogues lengthen faster than standards mature, and the fragmentation that integration was meant to solve remains, in many respects, intact. The review that follows takes this tension as its starting point: it surveys the available software landscape across general-purpose frameworks, microbiome-centred tools, GUI platforms and containerised infrastructure, examines the limited but informative benchmarking evidence, and uses EasyMultiProfiler as a worked example of what a domain-specific, workflow-level solution can — and cannot — deliver relative to its alternatives.

A useful organizing principle for the heterogeneous landscape of multi-omics integration software is the point in the analytical pipeline at which information from different omics layers is allowed to interact. Three regimes are routinely distinguished in the methodological literature: early integration, in which raw or preprocessed features from each omics layer are concatenated into a single matrix and fed to one downstream learner; intermediate integration, in which each omics is first summarized in its own representation and the resulting views are then fused in a joint latent space, graph, or factor decomposition; and late integration, in which omics-specific models are trained independently and their outputs are combined only at the decision or prediction stage. This taxonomy, while inevitably simplified, maps cleanly onto the principal algorithmic families represented in the corpus reviewed here, and it provides a frame against which claims of methodological novelty can be assessed.

Early integration remains the most straightforward strategy and the easiest to implement on top of generic machine-learning toolkits. In its classical form it underlies pipelines that learn patient embeddings or disease classifiers directly from concatenated feature vectors. The contrastive adversarial encoder CAEncoder treats the integrated matrix as input to a Vision Transformer trained end-to-end against a CycleGAN-based adversarial objective [R30]. The appeal of this regime lies in its simplicity and in its compatibility with any supervised learner; its principal weaknesses, by contrast, are the curse of dimensionality when omics blocks differ in scale and the implicit assumption that cross-omics interactions can be captured by a single monolithic model.

Intermediate integration has become the dominant paradigm in bulk and single-cell multi-omics research. The most influential instances are joint matrix-factorization methods, similarity-based fusion algorithms, and conceptual frameworks that combine per-omics representations with downstream multi-omics analyses. The MOADLN framework uses self-attention to capture patient correlations and a Multi-Omics Correlation Discovery Network to learn cross-omic label correlations for biomedical data classification [R17]. The MOFA family and its transfer-learning extension MOTL exemplify the factor-analytic branch, projecting each omics into a shared low-dimensional space whose factors can be annotated biologically and used for downstream clustering or regression [R32]. Similarity network fusion and its descendants constitute a parallel branch that constructs per-omics patient graphs and iteratively fuses them into a single affinity matrix; in the recent benchmarking of eight representative early, intermediate and late integration methods on TCGA colorectal cancer data, SNF emerged as the strongest performer on both simulated and real-world datasets [R4]. Conceptual schemes such as STATegra formalize the intermediate regime by stepwise combining a per-omics machine-learning component analysis with a non-parametric data-combination step and multi-omics exploratory analysis [R24]. A more recent wave of intermediate methods adds deep representation learning to this template. DeepMoIC uses autoencoders to obtain compact per-omics embeddings and then incorporates a patient similarity network through a graph-convolutional architecture [R12]; MCluster-VAEs employs a unified variational autoencoder with an attention mechanism to learn cluster-friendly representations in an end-to-end fashion [R22]; MoAGL-SA generates patient graphs from each omics with graph learning and uses self-attention to weight per-omics graph embeddings adaptively before classification [R39]; MO-GCAN combines per-omics graph convolutional networks with a sample-fusion graph attention network for supervised subtyping across eight cancer types [R29]; and TMODINET adds a Dirichlet-based uncertainty estimation head to a self-attention and graph-convolutional backbone to address the trustworthiness of predictions in clinical settings [R9]. The supervised feature-selection framework DIABLO from the mixOmics package sits at the boundary of intermediate and supervised integration, since it constructs sparse latent components that are jointly predictive of phenotypic groups while remaining interpretable as correlated biomarker signatures; the same joint-decomposition philosophy underlies several of the survival-prediction benchmarks that combine per-omics regularized regressions at the score level [R27, R46].

Late integration, in which each omics produces its own prediction that is then aggregated, is conceptually the most modular and the least prone to dominance by the highest-variance view. Software-side support for late fusion is less conspicuous than for the other two regimes, but it is implicitly used whenever pipelines train separate per-omics classifiers or survival models and combine them at the score level, as in parts of the multi-omics biomarker benchmark that compared 20 statistical, machine-learning and deep-learning methods against gold-standard prognostic and therapeutic biomarkers across five cancer datasets [R50]. The reduced representation of each omics to a prediction score also makes late integration attractive when cohorts are partially overlapping and omics blocks differ in availability.

A second axis that cuts orthogonally across this pipeline taxonomy is the degree of supervision. Unsupervised methods dominate the discovery-oriented literature, where the goal is subtype identification, dimensionality reduction or biomarker prioritization without external labels; representative tools include SNF [R4], MOFA and MOTL [R32], MCluster-VAEs [R22] and the CancerSubtypes package that wraps four unsupervised subtype-discovery approaches with standardized preprocessing [R49]. Supervised methods, in turn, are preferred when gold-standard endpoints such as cancer subtype, drug response or survival are available; DIABLO [R27], MOADLN [R17], MO-GCAN [R29], TMODINET [R9] and the survival-prediction benchmark that evaluated 11 methods across 18 TCGA datasets all belong to this category [R46]. The systematic survival benchmark is notable because it reported that only one of the multi-omics methods, block forest, outperformed a clinical Cox model, providing one of the few head-to-head empirical demonstrations that more elaborate integration architectures do not always yield better predictions than simpler baselines [R46].

Single-cell multimodal integration adds a third dimension to this scheme because it must reconcile modalities measured on the same cell, on matched cells across modalities, or on different cells within a population. The benchmark of 14 protein-abundance prediction algorithms and 18 single-cell integration algorithms on 47 datasets found totalVI and scArches to be the top protein predictors and Seurat, MOJITOO and scAI to be the strongest vertical integrators [R10], while a parallel benchmark of 12 multi-omics integration methods on RNA and ATAC data emphasized that no single method dominates across the six evaluation aspects considered [R37]. Domain-specific tools such as scMGAT for joint RNA, protein, methylation and ATAC integration [R51] and ScSmOP for single-cell single-molecule multiomics data [R19] further populate this niche.

A critical reading of the literature reveals two persistent limitations of the proposed taxonomy. First, the same architectural template, most prominently the combination of graph attention networks with per-omics encoders, is re-instantiated with minor variations across cancers, omics combinations and prediction tasks [R12, R29, R39, R42, R51], and the accompanying papers typically demonstrate improvement over a small, often self-curated, baseline set rather than over state-of-the-art supervised or factor-analytic methods evaluated under matched conditions. Second, claims about the superiority of early, intermediate or late fusion are rarely supported by rigorous head-to-head evaluation: the CRC benchmark [R4], the survival benchmark [R46], the single-cell integration benchmarks [R10, R37] and the multi-omics biomarker benchmark [R50] all show that the relative ranking of integration strategies is dataset-dependent, and that simpler early or late approaches can be competitive with, or superior to, more elaborate intermediate models in specific settings. The taxonomy is therefore best used as a descriptive device rather than as evidence for any universal methodological hierarchy.

General-purpose integration frameworks can be grouped along a continuum from tools that genuinely abstract the integration step—exposing it as a swappable component in a wider workflow—to packages that hard-wire a single algorithm and treat preprocessing or visualization as the only configurable layer. The most useful abstractions decouple three concerns: the data container, the integration operator, and the downstream statistical or biological interpretation. The R/Bioconductor ecosystem has been particularly fertile for this style of design. The moiraine package builds reproducible multi-omics pipelines that preprocess heterogeneous omics layers, dispatch them to one or more user-chosen integration methods, and return standardized outputs so that results can be compared across algorithms [R3]. Similarly, miodin offers a workflow-based syntax in which the same pipeline language supports vertical integration (same samples profiled on different platforms) and horizontal integration (same variables measured across studies), enabling transparent re-use of the same analysis scaffolding across transcriptomics, genomics and proteomics [R48]. timeOmics extends this philosophy to temporal designs—providing preprocessing, modeling and clustering of longitudinal multi-omics data and demonstrating it on the integrative Human Microbiome Project diabetes dataset combining mRNA, metabolites, gut taxa and clinical variables [R20]—while its companion netOmics builds hybrid multi-omics networks with smart node labeling and propagation to extract interpretable relationships from the same kind of data [R21]. These four packages share the property that the integration algorithm is an explicit, named object in the workflow: the user is not buying a single method but a methodology-neutral execution engine.

A second tier of R packages is method-centric yet generalizable, exposing a single integrative operator but with rich preprocessing, validation and visualization surrounding it. mixOmics and its supervised DIABLO extension [R27] form the canonical example, with reproducible workflows demonstrated for plant multi-omics under abiotic stress combining phenomics, metabolomics, proteomics and transcriptomics [R16]. CancerSubtypes packages four established subtype-identification algorithms behind a common interface, allowing feature selection, validation and biological follow-up to be swapped in and out [R49]. MUUMI sits between these tiers: it is presented as a unified R framework for statistical meta-analysis coupled with similarity network fusion and molecular interactome inference, but its integration layer is essentially fixed—the value-add is the coupling of meta-analysis to network interpretation rather than algorithm interchangeability [R2]. FindIT2 occupies a more specialized niche, providing a complete framework for TF target inference from ChIP-seq/ATAC-seq and RNA-seq that is highly generalizable across species but constrained to a single biological question [R45]. The Python side is currently less populated by neutral abstraction layers and more by deep-learning frameworks with fixed graph architectures, exemplified by BioNeuralNet, a modular graph neural network framework for end-to-end network-based multi-omics analysis [R5].

The benchmarking literature tempers expectations about the relative merit of these approaches. A large-scale study of 11 survival prediction methods across 18 TCGA multi-omics datasets found that methods explicitly accounting for multi-omics group structure performed only marginally better than naive single-block baselines, and only the block-forest variant—a tree-based ensemble that respects block boundaries—meaningfully outperformed a clinical Cox model [R46]. A benchmark of eight early, intermediate and late integration methods for colorectal cancer subtyping identified similarity network fusion (SNF) as the top performer across simulated and real-world datasets [R4]. A separate study benchmarking 20 statistical, machine-learning and deep-learning methods against gold-standard prognostic and therapeutic biomarkers ranked DeePathNet and DeepKEGG as top performers [R50]. The implication is sobering for the deep-learning community: statistical and machine-learning methods (boosting, penalized regression, random forest) implemented with a comparatively small methodological footprint remain competitive with far more elaborate architectures on tabular multi-omics data, and the additional complexity of graph attention, variational autoencoders or cycleGAN-based encoders is rarely justified by accuracy alone on cancer benchmarks.

Several limitations cut across this whole class of tools. First, the abstraction layers—moiraine, miodin, timeOmics—are R-centric, which makes them composable with the Bioconductor infrastructure (MultiAssayExperiment, SummarizedExperiment) but more difficult to weave into Python ecosystems that increasingly dominate deep-learning for omics. Second, the more specialized packages such as MUUMI, CancerSubtypes or the NMF-plus-metaheuristic framework combining adaptive gorilla troops optimization with sparse-joint NMF for cancer subtyping [R43] often lack head-to-head comparisons against the algorithms they are intended to complement, so claims of added value rest on demonstration rather than systematic benchmarking. Third, most frameworks are validated on a small number of case studies (IPF transcriptomes and THP-1 macrophages for MUUMI [R2]; Arabidopsis stress data for mixOmics [R16]; iHMP diabetes for timeOmics [R20]; TCGA glioblastoma and melanoma for the STATegra framework [R24]), which limits generalizability. The narrow evidence base and the absence of matched-condition head-to-head benchmarks across this entire class—including the Bioconductor-based microbiome workflows discussed later—mean that tool choice in practice rests on scope and infrastructure fit rather than demonstrated superiority on any standardized workload.
